events.text: The letter is short and very polite, which is how you know it is serious. A house you owe has decided it is time. The seal at the bottom is the one you put your own name beside, years ago.

choices.text: Read it twice and put it where you will see it

effects.log: You put it on the table where you eat. Every meal, it looks at you.

choices.text: Ask the messenger what they really want

effects.log: The messenger smiles and says the letter says everything. It does not, and you both know it.

choices.text: Tell the messenger you will answer within the year

effects.log: The messenger bows and goes. A year is a long time, and not long at all.

events.text: A guest from a house you owe sits in your hall and talks about the weather for an hour. Then, standing to leave, the guest mentions the old favour, as if it had only just come to mind.

choices.text: Walk the guest to the gate

effects.log: At the gate the guest bows and says your house was always a good friend. It sounds like a reminder.

choices.text: Say plainly that you remember

effects.log: The guest looks relieved, and a little sorry to have had to ask.

choices.text: Change the subject back to the weather

effects.log: The guest laughs, and lets you. The letter that follows a week later does not.

events.text: Debts between houses are not written in ink but in who stands beside whom. Today a house you owe has sent word: it needs someone to stand beside it.

choices.text: Count what you owe them

effects.log: You count. It is more than you remembered, and less than they will.

choices.text: Ask the oldest people you know what was promised

effects.log: The oldest of them remembers the day exactly, and tells it in a way that makes you sit up.

choices.text: Sleep on it

effects.log: You sleep on it badly.

events.text: The exchange is held on the old field between the two houses, as it has been for longer than either remembers. Three a side, the juniors bow, and the elders on both stands pretend not to care who wins.

choices.text: Watch the elders instead of the field

effects.log: The elders on both stands care very much. You learn more about the houses from their faces than from the fighting.

choices.text: Cheer for your own, loudly

effects.log: The juniors hear you. One of them stands a little straighter.

choices.text: Go and speak to the other house's juniors after

effects.log: They are wary, then friendly. Exchanges are for this too.

variants: The old field between the two houses is roped off again for the exchange. Three a side, bows all round, and on the stands the elders of both houses study the clouds with great interest.
Exchange day. The juniors of both houses line up on the old field, too stiff to look at each other, and the elders on the stands talk loudly about the weather and watch every move.
Banners on both sides of the old field, three juniors a side, a judge who has done this forty times. The bows are deep and careful. Everyone on the stands is very busy not caring who wins.
The two houses meet on the old field for the exchange, as their grandparents did. The juniors bow too low; the elders pretend to be bored; a dog runs across the field and is cheered by both sides.

events.text: Every few years the rival houses send their young ones to test each other, politely, in front of everyone. This year's exchange draws a crowd from three towns, and a man selling roasted chestnuts makes his fortune.

choices.text: Buy chestnuts for the juniors

effects.log: They eat them in a row on the bench, and look younger than they fought.

choices.text: Note who on the other side is worth watching

effects.log: Two names go into your memory. One day they will be elders.

choices.text: Bow to the other house's head when it is over

effects.log: The bow is returned, exactly as deep. That is the whole point.

variants: The rival houses send their young to test each other again, politely and in public. The crowd comes from three towns this time, and someone has set up a stall of hot buns at the edge of the field.
It is an exchange year. Both houses pretend it is nothing, and both have trained for it all spring. The field fills with townsfolk by noon, and the chestnut seller is back, richer than last time.

Another exchange between the rival houses, and the town treats it as a fair day. Children sit on the walls, the chestnut seller has hired a boy, and the young ones of both houses are pale with nerves.
The rival houses test their young again, in public and with perfect manners. Half the county has come to watch, and a story-seller is already telling last time's bouts, improved.

events.text: The exchange ends the way they always do: the winners trying not to look pleased, the losers trying not to look anything, and the two heads drinking tea together as if nothing had happened at all.

choices.text: Join the heads for tea

effects.log: The tea is very good and the talk is very careful. You leave knowing a little more about the other house.

choices.text: Find the junior who lost the last bout

effects.log: You tell them what they did well. They will remember who said it.

choices.text: Leave before the speeches

effects.log: You miss the speeches. Nobody misses you.

variants: The last bout is over. The winners try hard not to grin, the losers try hard not to show anything, and the two heads sit down to tea together as if nobody had fought at all.
The exchange ends as they all end: bows, a little stiff; a junior on one side trying not to cry; and the two heads pouring each other tea and talking about rain.
When the field is empty the two heads walk off together, side by side, discussing the price of rice. Behind them their juniors are still not looking at each other, and will not for a year.
It is over. Somebody won, by a little. The heads exchange the usual compliments over tea, and the juniors who lost are already planning the next exchange in whispers.

events.text: The basin is gold and full of clear water, and the hall is full of witnesses from a dozen houses. When your hands come out of the water, everyone watching has agreed to something: your quarrels are over, theirs with you too.

choices.text: Bow to the witnesses

effects.log: They bow back, house by house. Some of them were your enemies this morning.

choices.text: Look for the faces that are not glad

effects.log: You find two. They will keep the rite because everyone saw it. That is what witnesses are for.

choices.text: Dry your hands slowly

effects.log: You dry them slowly. It feels like setting something down that you had carried so long you forgot its weight.

events.text: An old rival comes to the rite, which nobody expected. When your hands are clean, the rival steps forward, bows, and says in front of everyone that the old matter between you is finished.

choices.text: Return the bow, as deep

effects.log: The hall breathes out. It is the best thing anyone has seen at a rite in years.

choices.text: Thank the rival for coming

effects.log: "I came to be sure," the rival says, and almost smiles.

choices.text: Say nothing, and nod

effects.log: A nod is enough. It is witnessed.

events.text: Washing your hands is easy. The hard part comes after, at the long table, where everyone you ever crossed swords with is eating your food and watching to see if you meant it.

choices.text: Mean it

effects.log: You mean it. By the end of the night, some of them believe you.

choices.text: Pour tea for the oldest enemy at the table

effects.log: The oldest enemy at the table lets you pour, and drinks it, and says nothing. It is a lot.

choices.text: Leave the table early and sit in the garden

effects.log: In the garden it is quiet. You find you are not sorry.
